profileText: A Representative from New York; was born in Williamstown, Mass., December 19, 1773; attended the common schools in Bennington, Vt.; moved with his parents to Troy, N.Y., in 1786; studied law; was admitted to the bar in 1795; commenced practice in Utica, N.Y.; assisted in the establishment of Utica ,N.Y., Public Library; librarian for a number of years; president of the village corporation; president of the Manhattan Bank, N.Y.; district attorney for the sixth district, 1801-1813; elected as a Democratic Republican to the Ninth Congress (March 4, 1805-March 3, 1807); served in the War of 1812; member of the New York state assembly, 1816-1818 and in 1819; regent of the University of the State of New York from January 28, 1817-February 13, 1824; district attorney of Oneida County 1818-1821; delegate to the New York state constitutional convention, 1821; judge of the circuit court, 1823-1833; appointed clerk of the New York state supreme court, 1834; moved to Geneva, Ontario County, N.Y., where he died; died on September 25, 1835, ; in Geneva, Ontario County, N.Y.; interment in the ``Burying Ground,'' Utica, Oneida County, N.Y.; reinterment in Forest Hill Cemetery, Utica, N.Y.

researchRecord.description: A letter from Jacob Jennings Brown to Nathan Williams or Thomas Childs written on August 30, 1814. In the letter, Jacob Brown writes Nathan Williams or Thomas Childs that he is on his way to Buffalo. He fears his militia will be deficient in arms, and asks that the keeper of the arsenal forward sufficient equipment. Jacob Brown was in command at the Battle of Niagara during the War of 1812.
